Notes

Etiology

CauseKey Points
Iatrogenic / ERCPPancreatic surgery/procedures; post-ERCP pancreatitis ≈5–7% (instrumentation, contrast injection, ductal pressure)
Hereditary — PRSS1Trypsinogen mutation → premature trypsin activation → autodigestion/recurrent pancreatitis
Hereditary — SPINK1Loss/impaired protease inhibition → recurrent enzyme activation
Duct obstructionNeoplasm or congenital anomaly — pancreas divisum: failed ductal fusion → drainage via duct of Santorini/minor papilla → relative obstruction
MetabolicHypertriglyceridemia (types I & V); hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia
OthersIschemia/hypoperfusion · smoking · infections
Drugs (≈1%)Thiazides, tetracycline, azathioprine, steroids, propofol (lipid-based anesthetic)
Idiopathic (≈15– 20%)Many apparently idiopathic cases have microlithiasis
POST-ERCP HYPERAMYLASEMIA
May occur without abdominal pain → hyperamylasemia alone, not necessarily clinical pancreatitis.
HEREDITARY PANCREATITIS
↑ risk of recurrent pancreatitis + pancreatic malignancy. Drugs are rare (≈1%) — think of common etiologies first.
  • Dark discolouration of the flanks → Grey Turner's sign (periumbilical = Cullen's). 439 ×4
Notes

Clinical Presentation & Diagnosis

PAIN
Abdominal pain = major presenting symptom; may be very severe/sharp and in different locations. Diagnosis is initially clinical + biochemical; imaging matters when diagnosis/etiology is unclear.
SEVERE ACUTE ABDOMINAL PAIN — DIFFERENTIAL
Acute pancreatitis · appendicitis · mesenteric vascular occlusion/ischemia.
Notes

Laboratory Findings

TestSignificance
Amylase + lipaseLipase is more specific; amylase also rises modestly (~200–300) in non-pancreatic conditions (see below)
GlucoseRises initially → usually normalizes unless underlying diabetes
CalciumFalls — calcium precipitation/fat saponification in necrosis
ABGImportant in severe disease — hypoxemia from pulmonary injury/ARDS; acid-base disturbance
WBC>16,000/mm³ = Ranson criterion
HematocritFall >10% during follow-up = Ranson criterion
PlateletsMay fall with significant bleeding
Non-Pancreatic Causes of Raised Amylase (~200–300)
• Head injury • Cholecystitis • Intestinal ischemia • Appendicitis• Hepatitis • Perforated viscus/peritonitis • Renal failure
★★★ NORMAL AMYLASE DESPITE ACUTE PANCREATITIS — 4 SITUATIONS
Still clinically suspected with normal amylase → CT may confirm the diagnosis. Delayed presentation >4 days — most common; serum amylase may have normalized, but urine amylase stays elevated up to ~10 days
1
Hemorrhagic pancreatitis
2
3 Acute-on-chronic pancreatitis
4 Hyperlipidemia-induced pancreatitis
Third spacing · vomiting · ↓ intake→Dehydration→Prerenal azotemia + electrolyte/acid-base (alkalosis/acidosis)
KEY STEP
Adequate fluid replacement is one of the most important initial management steps.
Normal amylase despite acute pancreatitis — 4 situations: (1) delayed presentation > 4 days (most common — urine amylase stays high ~10 days), (2) haemorrhagic, (3) acute-on-chronic, (4) hyperlipidaemia-induced → CT confirms.
  • Acute pancreatitis, vomiting → hypocalcaemia 437; blood abnormality keyed hypoglycaemia in one recall — the doctor: glucose rises (hyperglycaemia). 432
  • Severe pancreatitis + sepsis with generalised oedema despite large IV volumes → third-space losses. 438 ×8
Notes

Imaging

INITIAL IMAGING APPROACH
Chest X-ray → initial assessment for thoracic complications · Ultrasound → primarily to find the cause (gallstones/biliary disease) · CT and MRI → specific indications, not routine for every patient.
ModalityFindings / Role
Chest X-rayARDS; reactive pleural effusion (subdiaphragmatic inflammation). Air under diaphragm → perforated viscus, not pancreatitis
Abdominal X-raySentinel loop · colon cut-off sign
UltrasoundDetects gallstones; assesses biliary tract/CBD
MRIRarely routine; differentiates fluid vs viable/necrotic tissue
  • Pain for 5 days, gallstones, normal CBC/LFTs, left pleural effusion → initial test urine amylase. 435 ×5
  • Epigastric pain, vomiting 5 days, tachycardia, high WBC and amylase → initial investigation erect chest X-ray (exclude perforation) 436 ×4; febrile, amylase 1854 → imaging to find the cause → abdominal ultrasound 438 ×9
  • Amylase only 250 with upper abdominal pain, normal CXR → keyed CT to confirm (other recalls keyed ultrasound). 435 ×4
Notes

CT Abdomen — Not Routine

INDICATIONS
Diagnosis uncertain
1
Etiology uncertain / suspected obstructing tumor
2
3 Severe/toxic patient — suspected necrosis
4 Suspected local complication, e.g. collection
WHY AVOID UNNECESSARY CT
IV contrast may worsen renal injury in dehydrated patients
Radiation ≈ ~500 chest X-rays
Clinical assessment remains essential — don't replace examination with repeated scans
INFECTED NECROSIS ON CT
CT may show pancreatic necrosis; gas bubbles within necrotic tissue → infected necrosis (bacterial translocation).
  • Necrotising pancreatitis with gas bubbles (infected necrosis) → IV antibiotics 437 ×2; 2 weeks after AP, fever + solid collection with gas → IV antibiotics, resuscitation and CT-guided aspiration (doctor-confirmed — necrosectomy is delayed). 442
Notes

Biliary Pancreatitis — CBD Stone Assessment

Stone passes / impacts LFTs rise→Stone passed LFTs fall over ~2–3 days·LFTs high ~3 days investigate retained CBD stone
TestRole
MRCPUseful non-invasive assessment of the biliary tree
EUSHighly accurate, especially for small CBD stones
ERCPPrincipally therapeutic — stone extraction (e.g. basket)
ERCP COMPLICATIONS
Acute/aggravated pancreatitis · bleeding · infection · cholangitis/cholecystitis · perforation — the most serious complication.
  • ERCP for CBD stones, severe epigastric pain to the back 6 h later → post-ERCP pancreatitis. 442 ×3
  • Gallstone pancreatitis with a dilated CBD (obstruction), no cholangitis → keyed ERCP. 442
Notes

Initial Management

FIRST: IS THE DIAGNOSIS CORRECT?
Treating a perforated viscus as pancreatitis may lead to sepsis/death. Disposition: mild → ward with close observation; severe/organ dysfunction → ICU. Ward patients can still deteriorate.
Notes

ABC

StepAction
AirwayAssess/protect, especially with ↓ consciousness
BreathingHypoxemia/ARDS; pulse oximetry; O₂ (~6 L/min when required)
CirculationAggressive but monitored fluid resuscitation
Notes

Fluids

LACTATED RINGER'S PREFERRED
LR preferred in acute pancreatitis because it reduces the systemic inflammatory response. Monitor with hemodynamics/vital signs, urine output + color, pulse oximetry. Elderly/cardiac → risk of overload → closer/central monitoring.
URINE OUTPUT TARGET
Adults ~0.5–1 mL/kg/hr
Children ≥1 mL/kg/hr
ONGOING GASTRIC LOSSES/VOMITING
Normal saline useful — replaces lost chloride/sodium.
Fluid (mmol/L)NaClLactateCa
Lactated Ringer's130109284
Normal saline154154——
Lactated Ringer's is preferred (reduces the systemic inflammatory response). Target urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/h (adults), ≥ 1 mL/kg/h (children). Ongoing vomiting → normal saline replaces chloride.
Notes

Analgesia

SEVERE PAIN → OPIOIDS
Opioid/narcotic analgesia. Lecture advised avoiding morphine (concern for sphincter spasm). NSAIDs not emphasized for severe pain.
Notes

Severity Assessment

Determines ward vs ICU, prognosis, expected complications and treatment intensity.

  • Blood test to assess severity → CRP 436; work-up that determines prognosis → keyed WBC count (a Ranson criterion). 431
Notes

Ranson Criteria ★★★

MOST EMPHASIZED EXAM SCORE
Assessed partly on admission and completed at 48 hours. Examples: WBC >16,000, hematocrit fall >10%. Separate criteria for gallstone vs non-gallstone pancreatitis.
Ranson ScoreSeverity
1–2Mild
≥3Moderate–severe — increasing morbidity/mortality with higher scores
Notes

Other Scores & Markers

ScoreKey Point
Modified GlasgowSimilar severity information to Ranson
APACHE IICommon in ICU; >8 = severe
BISAPSimple bedside index — easier but less accurate
CRPSupports severity assessment
Balthazar / CTSICT inflammation + extent of necrosis; accurate — but don't order CT solely to calculate it
SOFAOrgan dysfunction; >2 / increasing organ involvement → significant systemic disease
Notes

Severity Classification

Mild→Moderate→Severe→Critical
AxisCategories
Local complicationsAbsent / present · sterile / infected
Systemic organ failureAbsent · transient (reverses with resuscitation, e.g. hypotension/renal dysfunction improving with fluids) · persistent (does not rapidly resolve)
failure.Mild = no significant local complication or persistent organ failure; the severe/critical end = infected local complications + persistent organ
Notes

Antibiotics, Recovery & Nutrition

NO ROUTINE PROPHYLACTIC ANTIBIOTICS
Give only with evidence of infection:
Cholangitis
Imaging suggesting infection
Positive aspiration/culture
Infected necrosis/abscess
DRUGS OF CHOICE
Imipenem / meropenem — good pancreatic penetration. Then adjust to the clinical/microbiological situation.
  • Necrotising pancreatitis — metabolic response → increased lipolysis 432 ×2; septic ventilated patient on inotropes 8 weeks after infected necrosis → hormone keyed glucagon (the source notes insulin rises physiologically). 434 ×2
Notes

Clinical Recovery

Reduced pain
Stable vital signs
Less tenderness
Falling labs/pancreatic enzymes
FAILURE TO IMPROVE
Reassess and investigate for complications or another diagnosis.
Notes

Nutrition

FEED EARLY
Start feeding early when clinically tolerated — routine NPO for 3–4 days to "rest the pancreas" is no longer favored. Don't force oral feeding with active vomiting. Prefer enteral nutrition.
TPN
Mainly for critically ill ICU patients who cannot be fed enterally. Disadvantages: central-line complications/infection, electrolyte/metabolic abnormalities, other PN complications.
  • Mild acute pancreatitis → enteral feeding, IV fluids, pain control (no TPN, no routine antibiotics). 441
Notes

Treat the Cause

SituationManagement
Gallstone pancreatitisCholecystectomy during the same admission when appropriate; in severe disease, timing depends on recovery/complications
Sterile necrosisPrimarily conservative; delay intervention when possible
Infected necrosisDrainage/debridement or necrosectomy; delay definitive surgery in stable cases ~8 weeks when feasible
  • Gallstones, 18 h of epigastric pain, mild cholestasis, stable → initial management IV crystalloids. 438 ×4
  • Mild gallstone pancreatitis (amylase 1253, normal LFTs) → cholecystectomy in the same admission. 442 ×9
Notes

Local Complications

Pancreatic / Peripancreatic Collections

Classified by early/acute vs later/chronic and fluid-only vs solid/necrotic content. Early collections occur within ~4 weeks; acute peripancreatic fluid collections in ~78% — many reabsorb spontaneously.

  • Afebrile, day 10, peripancreatic fluid collection without a capsule → supportive care and observation. 442
Notes

Pancreatic Pseudocyst

DEFINITION
Pancreatic fluid collection with a mature wall but WITHOUT epithelial lining; develops after several weeks and often communicates with the pancreatic duct.
SYMPTOMS (~5–6 WEEKS)
Persistent abdominal pain
Postprandial vomiting
Gastric fullness/early satiety
CLASSIC INTERVENTION CRITERIA
Symptomatic
Size >6 cm
Persistence >6 weeks (modern: observe up to ~12 weeks)
ASYMPTOMATIC PSEUDOCYST
Do not intervene simply because it exists.
  • Pseudocyst — indication for surgical intervention → gastric/duodenal obstruction. 441
Notes

Drainage Options

ApproachDetails
1. Endoscopic transgastricCurrent preferred/gold standard — communication with stomach + drain/stent
2. SurgicalOpen/laparoscopic internal drainage: cystogastrostomy or cystoduodenostomy; evacuate/wash; obtain wall tissue — may be a cystic pancreatic neoplasm
3. PercutaneousLess preferred — recurrence, infection, external pancreatic fistula; for selected high-risk patients
Notes

Pancreatic Abscess / Infected Collection

Worsening pain + leukocytosis/sepsis→Percutaneous drainage→Unsuitable/failed surgical drainage/debridement
Notes

Pancreatic Ascites / Pleural Effusion

MECHANISM & DIAGNOSIS
After severe/necrotizing pancreatitis: pancreatic duct disruption/leak; may present weeks–months later. Aspirate → markedly ↑ amylase (~3,000). Pleural fluid: same leak mechanism.
CONSERVATIVE FIRST (~95% RESOLVE)
Drain symptomatic fluid
Octreotide
TPN / pancreatic rest
Surgery for persistent leak/failure.
  • Ascites 2 months after severe alcoholic pancreatitis — confirming the cause → keyed CT (paracentesis with ascitic amylase is the classic test). 439
Notes

Hemorrhagic / Vascular Complications

PSEUDOANEURYSM
Inflammation damages adjacent vessels → pseudoaneurysm → major hemorrhage into the peritoneal cavity, the pancreatic duct (hemosuccus pancreaticus), or the GI tract.
Splenic vein thrombosis→Left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension→Gastric varices→Splenectomy if symptomatic/bleeding
  • Recurrent pancreatitis, bleeding isolated fundal varices, thrombosed splenic vein, normal portal vein → splenectomy. 435 ×8
Notes

Systemic Complications / Organ Failure

Cardiovascular

Renal CNS

Respiratory

Coagulation Hepatic

MORTALITY
Significant organ failure → ICU support. Mortality rises with the number and duration of failed organs — ~91% in very severe multi-organ failure.
Notes

Chronic Pancreatitis

ETIOLOGY
Causes generally overlap with acute pancreatitis — alcohol = most common cause emphasized in the lecture.
  • Most common cause of acute pancreatitis → gallstones. 441
Notes

Clinical Features

FeatureDetails
PainChronic/recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back; may persist for years, then "burn-out" — decreases/disappears as destruction progresses
Exocrine dysfunctionDiarrhea/steatorrhea + malnutrition
Endocrine dysfunctionDiabetes mellitus
MalignancyRisk of pancreatic cancer
  • Acute epigastric pain radiating to the back + vomiting ×6, epigastric tenderness → acute pancreatitis. 438 ×5
  • Recurrent epigastric pain, steatorrhoea, new diabetes, calcifications on CT → chronic pancreatitis 442 ×2; steatorrhoea = loss of exocrine function 441; alcoholic with dilated ducts → alcohol cessation + pancreatic enzyme replacement. 442
Notes

Complications

Pseudocyst

Pleural effusion

Exocrine insufficiency → malnutrition Pancreatic malignancy

Abscess / infected collection Pancreatic ascites

Endocrine insufficiency → diabetes

Notes

Investigation

CT ABDOMEN
Assesses pancreatic morphology/complications — particularly when there is concern for malignancy. New/changed symptoms → further imaging to exclude complications or neoplasm.
MRCP
Evaluates pancreatic duct anatomy/obstruction; may be used for follow-up ductal assessment.
Notes

Pain Management

Analgesics→Opioids · transdermal patches pain/anesthesia service→Celiac plexus block→Surgery if medical/endoscopic fails
CELIAC PLEXUS BLOCK / NEUROLYSIS
For pain persisting despite medical treatment. EUS or CT guided; local anesthetic around the celiac plexus; alcohol injection → neurolysis. Relief for several months — ~4–8 months. Also used for pancreatic cancer pain.
Notes

Surgery

MAIN INDICATION
Failure of medical/endoscopic pain management.
Disease PatternProcedure
Dilated main duct >8 mmPuestow (lateral pancreaticojejunostomy) — longitudinally open/decompress the duct and drain it into jejunum
Non-dilated duct / localizedDrainage less suitable → resection by site of disease; body/tail → distal pancreatectomy
Severe refractory/extensiveSubtotal/total pancreatectomy — last resort, rare, selected cases
PRESERVE PANCREATIC TISSUE
Extensive resection → loss of endocrine tissue → insulin deficiency with brittle diabetes; after total/near-total pancreatectomy → insulin therapy with marked glucose fluctuations.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 Post-ERCP pancreatitis ≈5–7%; post-ERCP hyperamylasemia without pain is not clinical pancreatitis
2 PRSS1 = trypsinogen mutation; SPINK1 = protease-inhibitor loss → recurrent pancreatitis + malignancy risk
3 Pancreas divisum → drainage via Santorini/minor papilla → relative obstruction
4 Drugs ≈1% (thiazides, tetracycline, azathioprine, steroids, propofol); idiopathic 15–20% — often microlithiasis
5 Lipase is more specific than amylase; amylase also rises (~200–300) with head injury, hepatitis, cholecystitis, perforation, ischemia, renal failure,
appendicitis
6 ★★★ Normal amylase despite pancreatitis: delayed >4 days (most common — urine amylase stays up ~10 days), hemorrhagic, acute-on-chronic,
hyperlipidemic → CT confirms
7 Glucose rises initially; calcium falls (fat saponification); ABG for hypoxemia/ARDS in severe disease
8 Air under the diaphragm = perforated viscus — rule it out before calling it pancreatitis
9 CT is not routine: only for uncertain diagnosis/etiology, suspected necrosis, or collections; gas in necrosis = infection
10 LFTs should fall over 2–3 days after stone passage; persistently high ~3 days → MRCP/EUS → ERCP
11 Lactated Ringer's preferred; target urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr (adults), ≥1 mL/kg/hr (children)
12 Ranson: admission + 48 h; 1–2 mild, ≥3 moderate–severe; separate gallstone/non-gallstone criteria
13 APACHE II >8 = severe; SOFA >2 = significant organ dysfunction; don't CT just for the Balthazar score
14 Severity = local complications (sterile/infected) + organ failure (transient vs persistent)
15 No prophylactic antibiotics; treat proven infection with imipenem/meropenem
16 Feed early, prefer enteral; TPN only when enteral feeding is impossible
17 Gallstone pancreatitis → cholecystectomy in the same admission; infected necrosis → delayed necrosectomy (~8 weeks)
18 Pseudocyst = mature wall, no epithelium; intervene if symptomatic, >6 cm, >6 weeks — endoscopic transgastric drainage first
19 Pancreatic ascites: amylase ~3,000; ~95% resolve with drainage + octreotide + TPN
20 Splenic vein thrombosis → sinistral portal hypertension → gastric varices → splenectomy
21 Chronic pancreatitis: alcohol most common; epigastric pain → back, steatorrhea, diabetes, cancer risk; CT for morphology/malignancy, MRCP for duct
22 Chronic pain: analgesia → opioids → celiac plexus neurolysis (~4–8 months) → surgery: duct >8 mm → Puestow; non-dilated → resection by site; total
pancreatectomy last resort → brittle diabetes
  • Recurrent attacks, cholecystectomy 30 years ago, long-standing alcohol, high amylase/lipase, normal bilirubin → alcoholic pancreatitis. 439
  • 5 weeks after AP: epigastric pain, post-prandial vomiting, tender epigastric mass → pseudocyst 439 ×4; treatment keyed percutaneous drainage (435) 435 ×4; 7-cm symptomatic pseudocyst at 6 weeks, afebrile → endoscopic drainage (doctor-confirmed). 442

Pancreas

Embryology of the Pancreas
Origin:
  • The pancreas develops in the 4th week of fetal life from dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds (outgrowths of the caudal foregut).
  • These buds rotate and fuse, forming the pancreas.
Derivatives of Pancreatic Buds:
  • Ventral pancreas → Uncinate process & caudal portion of head.
  • Dorsal pancreas → Cranial portion of head, body, and tail.
Duct Formation:
  • Main pancreatic duct (Duct of Wirsung) → Formed by the fusion of ventral and dorsal ducts.
  • Accessory pancreatic duct (Duct of Santorini) → Remnant of the dorsal duct.
  • Pancreas divisum (5-10% of population) → Failure of duct fusion, leading to separate drainage.
Anatomy of the Pancreas
Location:
  • Retroperitoneal organ located in the upper abdomen, extending from the duodenum (head) to the splenic hilum (tail).
  • Anteriorly: Stomach, duodenum.
  • Posteriorly: Aorta, IVC, left kidney, adrenal gland.
Pancreatic Duct System:
  • Main pancreatic duct (Duct of Wirsung) → Joins the common bile duct at the ampulla of Vater, draining into the duodenum.
  • Accessory pancreatic duct (Duct of Santorini) → Drains separately into the duodenum.
Blood Supply:
  • Head → Pancreaticoduodenal arteries (branches of celiac & superior mesenteric arteries).
  • Body & Tail → Splenic artery (branches: dorsal pancreatic, pancreatica magna, caudal pancreatic).
Lymphatic Drainage:
  • Peripancreatic nodes → Celiac & superior mesenteric lymph nodes.
Innervation:
  • Parasympathetic (Vagus nerve) → Stimulates secretion.
  • Sympathetic (Splanchnic nerves) → Regulates vascular tone.
Physiology of the Pancreas
1- Exocrine Function
  • Role: Secretes digestive enzymes & bicarbonate into the duodenum.
  • Stimulated by:
  • Secretin (in response to acidic chyme) → Increases bicarbonate secretion.
  • Cholecystokinin (CCK) (in response to fats & proteins) → Increases enzyme secretion.
  • Vagal stimulation → Enhances secretion.
Pancreatic Juice Composition:
  • Enzymes:
  • Amylase → Digests carbohydrates.
  • Lipase → Digests fats.
  • Proteases (Trypsinogen, Chymotrypsinogen, Procarboxypeptidase) → Activated in the duodenum by enterokinase.

Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) → Neutralizes gastric acid.

  • Protective Mechanisms Against Autodigestion:
  • Enzymes stored as inactive zymogens.
  • Protease inhibitors prevent premature activation.
  • Enzymes activated only in the duodenum.
2- Endocrine Function
Hormones Secreted by the Islets of Langerhans:
  • Insulin (β-cells, 70%) → ↓ Blood glucose (anabolic hormone).
  • Glucagon (α-cells, 20%) → ↑ Blood glucose (catabolic hormone).
  • Somatostatin (δ-cells, 5%) → Inhibits insulin, glucagon, and digestive enzymes.
  • Pancreatic polypeptide (PP cells) → Regulates pancreatic secretions.

Regulation:

Insulin Secretion Stimulated By:

  • Glucose, amino acids, fatty acids.
  • Secretin, CCK, gastrin.
Glucagon Secretion Stimulated By:
  • Low blood glucose, amino acids, catecholamines.
  • Inhibited by insulin & hyperglycemia.
Congenital Pancreatic Abnormalities
1- Pancreas Divisum
  • Cause: Failure of dorsal & ventral pancreatic duct fusion.
  • Consequence: Most of the pancreas drains through the minor papilla, which may lead to pancreatitis.
  • Diagnosis: MRCP or ERCP.
  • Treatment: Endoscopic minor papilla stenting (if symptomatic).
2- Annular Pancreas
  • Cause: Failure of the ventral pancreatic bud to rotate properly, forming a ring around the duodenum.
  • Presentation:
  • Infants → Duodenal obstruction (bilious vomiting, double bubble sign on X-ray).
  • Adults → Chronic abdominal pain, nausea, pancreatitis.
  • Diagnosis: CT scan, Upper GI series.
  • Treatment: Duodenojejunostomy (bypass procedure). Resection is avoided due to the risk of fistula formation.
Pancreatitis

Pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas caused by premature activation of digestive enzymes leading to autodigestion, fibrosis, and loss of function.

Types:

1. Acute Pancreatitis (AP) → Sudden onset, potential for complete resolution.

2. Chronic Pancreatitis (CP) → Persistent inflammation causing permanent

  • damage, fibrosis, and loss of function.
Major Clinical Features:
  • Acute Pancreatitis → Severe epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, elevated serum amylase & lipase.
  • Chronic Pancreatitis → Recurrent pain, pancreatic calcifications, steatorrhea, diabetes mellitus.
Special Types:
  • Recurrent acute pancreatitis (RAP) → Multiple acute attacks without permanent damage.
  • Subacute pancreatitis → Milder, prolonged attacks (seen in alcohol- induced pancreatitis).
Causes of Pancreatitis
1️- Metabolic Causes
Alcohol (40-50% of cases in the U.S.)
  • Long-term alcohol use (≥6 years) damages pancreatic ducts & increases enzyme activation.
  • Can cause acute & chronic pancreatitis, progressing to fibrosis.
Hyperlipidemia (Triglycerides > 1,000 mg/dL)
  • High triglycerides → Lipoprotein degradation → Free fatty acids → Direct pancreatic injury.
  • Common in familial hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, obesity.
Hypercalcemia (e.g., Hyperparathyroidism, Malignancies)
  • High calcium activates pancreatic enzymes prematurely → Inflammation.
  • Chronic cases develop calcific pancreatitis & pancreatic stones.
Drug-Induced Pancreatitis
  • Most common drugs → Corticosteroids, azathioprine, thiazide diuretics, tetracyclines, estrogens, valproic acid.
  • Mechanism: Toxic injury, ischemia, metabolic disruption.
Scorpion Venom
  • Certain species (e.g., Tityus trinitatis) stimulate massive pancreatic enzyme secretion, leading to acute pancreatitis.
2️- Mechanical Causes
Gallstones & Biliary Pancreatitis (~50% of cases)
  • Transient obstruction of the ampulla of Vater by gallstones/sludge leads to bile reflux into the pancreatic duct, triggering enzyme activation.
  • Clues: Jaundice, elevated ALT > 3x normal suggests biliary origin.
Pancreatic Duct Obstruction
  • Causes: Pancreatic tumors, pancreatic divisum, post-surgical strictures, trauma.
  • Leads to backpressure, enzyme activation, and inflammation.
ERCP-Induced Pancreatitis
  • Occurs in ~5% of patients after endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).
  • Risk factors: Difficult bile duct cannulation, sphincterotomy, contrast injection into the pancreatic duct.
3️- Vascular & Autoimmune Causes
Vascular Insufficiency
  • Ischemia due to atherosclerosis, embolism, periarteritis nodosa can damage the pancreas.
  • Seen in post-cardiac surgery patients receiving high-dose calcium chloride.
Autoimmune Pancreatitis
  • IgG4-related disease causing diffuse inflammation & fibrosis.
  • Presents with painless jaundice, pancreatic enlargement, weight loss.
  • Responds to corticosteroids.
4️- Infectious Causes
Mumps Virus (Most Common Viral Cause)
  • Mumps can cause pancreatic inflammation → Seen in children & young adults.
Other Infectious Agents
  • Coxsackie B virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Cryptococcus, Mycoplasma, Ascaris lumbricoides (parasitic).
5️- Genetic Causes
Hereditary Pancreatitis
  • Due to PRSS1 mutation (autosomal dominant).
  • Causes early-onset pancreatitis (<20 years) with a high risk of pancreatic cancer.
Cystic Fibrosis (CFTR mutation)
  • Thick mucus obstructs pancreatic ducts, leading to chronic pancreatitis & exocrine insufficiency.
SPINK1 Mutation
  • Defective trypsin inhibitor → Premature enzyme activation.
Clinical Features of Acute vs. Chronic Pancreatitis
  • Feature Acute Pancreatitis (AP) Chronic Pancreatitis (CP)
OnsetSudden, severeGradual, recurrent
PainSevere epigastric pain, radiates to backRecurrent dull epigastric pain
Amylase/LipaseElevated (3x normal)Mild elevation or normal
ImagingCT shows enlarged pancreas, peripancreatic fat strandingCalcifications, dilated ducts, atrophy
ComplicationsPseudocysts, necrosis, ARDSSteatorrhea, diabetes,
pancreatic cancer
Diagnosis of Pancreatitis
Diagnosis of Acute Pancreatitis (Requires 2/3 Criteria)
  • Characteristic epigastric pain (radiates to back).
  • Serum lipase/amylase >3x normal.
  • Imaging findings (CT/MRI).
Tests for Etiology
  • Ultrasound → Detects gallstones.
  • CT scan → Identifies necrosis, pseudocysts.
  • MRCP/ERCP → Identifies ductal strictures, stones, pancreas divisum.
  • Triglyceride levels (>1,000 mg/dL suggests hyperlipidemic pancreatitis).
  • IgG4 levels (Autoimmune pancreatitis).
Management of Acute Pancreatitis
1️- Initial Supportive Care
  • NPO (Nil Per Os) → Rest the pancreas.
  • Aggressive IV Fluids (Lactated Ringer’s > Normal Saline).
  • Pain Control (IV opioids like fentanyl, morphine).
  • Oxygen & monitor for complications (ARDS, shock).
2️- Specific Treatments Based on Cause
  • Biliary Pancreatitis → Cholecystectomy after resolution.
  • Hypertriglyceridemia → Plasmapheresis if severe (>1,000 mg/dL).
  • Autoimmune Pancreatitis → Steroids (Prednisone 40 mg daily).
  • ERCP-Induced Pancreatitis → IV fluids, rectal NSAIDs for prevention.
Complications of Pancreatitis
Early (<1 Week)Late (>1 Week)
SIRS, ARDSPancreatic pseudocyst
Hypotension, AKINecrotizing pancreatitis
DIC, metabolic acidosisPancreatic abscess, sepsis
  • Pseudocyst → Collection of fluid, enzymes, & debris. If >6 cm & symptomatic, requires drainage.
  • Necrotizing Pancreatitis → Infected necrosis may need surgical debridement.
Acute Pancreatitis
  • Acute pancreatitis is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas due to autodigestion by pancreatic enzymes.
  • It ranges from mild interstitial edema to severe necrotizing pancreatitis with systemic complications.
Common Causes:
  • Gallstones (~50%)
  • Alcohol (~40%)
  • Hypertriglyceridemia (>1000 mg/dL)
  • Medications (steroids, azathioprine, thiazides, estrogens, tetracyclines, valproic acid)
  • ERCP-induced pancreatitis
  • Autoimmune pancreatitis (IgG4-related disease)
Clinical Features of Acute Pancreatitis
Symptoms:
  • Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back (worsens with eating).
  • Nausea & vomiting.
  • Fever, tachycardia, dehydration, hypotension in severe cases.
Signs:
  • Epigastric tenderness with guarding.
  • Absent bowel sounds (due to ileus).
  • Grey Turner Sign (flank ecchymosis) & Cullen’s Sign (periumbilical ecchymosis) → indicates hemorrhagic pancreatitis.
  • Pleural effusion (L > R) due to pancreatic exudates.
Diagnosis of Acute Pancreatitis
  • Diagnosis requires ≥2 of the following (Atlanta Criteria):
  • Epigastric pain consistent with acute pancreatitis.
  • Serum amylase or lipase >3x upper limit of normal.
  • Imaging findings (CT/MRI) of pancreatic inflammation.
  • Laboratory Tests:
  • Serum Lipase → Most specific marker. Elevated for several days.
  • Serum Amylase → Less specific (can be elevated in cholecystitis, perforated ulcers, intestinal ischemia).
  • Hypocalcemia → Saponification (calcium binds free fatty acids).
  • Elevated Hematocrit → Suggests dehydration & pancreatic necrosis.
  • Leukocytosis & CRP >150 mg/L → Indicates severe pancreatitis.
  • LFTs (ALT >150 IU/L) → Suggests biliary pancreatitis.
  • Imaging Studies:
  • CT scan with IV Contrast → Best for assessing necrosis, pseudocysts, and complications.
  • Ultrasound → First-line for gallstones & biliary obstruction.
  • MRI/MRCP → For detecting pancreatic duct abnormalities & pancreas divisum.

Management of Acute Pancreatitis
1️- Initial Supportive Care
  • NPO (Nil Per Os) → Rest the pancreas.
  • IV Fluids (Lactated Ringer’s > Normal Saline) to prevent hypovolemia & organ failure.
  • Pain Control (IV opioids → fentanyl, hydromorphone).
  • Oxygen & Monitoring for complications (ARDS, AKI, MODS).
Early aggressive IV hydration is most beneficial within the first 24 hours!
2️- Specific Management Based on Cause
  • Biliary Pancreatitis → ERCP if obstructed CBD & cholangitis.
  • Hypertriglyceridemia → Plasmapheresis if >1000 mg/dL.
  • Autoimmune Pancreatitis → Steroids (Prednisone 40 mg daily).
  • ERCP-Induced Pancreatitis → IV fluids, rectal NSAIDs to prevent it.
3️- Nutrition & Antibiotics
  • Early Enteral Feeding (via NJ tube) Preferred Over TPN.
  • Avoid routine antibiotics unless there’s infected necrosis (gas in pancreas on CT).
When to start feeding?
  • Mild pancreatitis → Start oral diet once nausea resolves.
  • Severe pancreatitis → NJ tube feeding within 24-48h.

Treatment of Acute Pancreatitis
A. Medical Treatment
  • Goals of medical therapy:
  • Reduce pancreatic secretory stimuli.
  • Correct fluid and electrolyte imbalances.
  • Prevent complications (organ failure, necrosis, infection, ARDS, etc.).
1️- Nutritional Support
  • Historically, patients were kept NPO (nothing by mouth) and given total parenteral nutrition (TPN).
  • Current guidelines: ✔ Early enteral feeding via a nasogastric (NG) or nasojejunal (NJ) tube is preferred to prevent gut atrophy & bacterial translocation. ✔ TPN only if ileus or intolerance to enteral feeding.
  • Benefits of Enteral Nutrition:
  • Reduces infection risk & organ failure.
  • Improves gut barrier integrity.
  • Lowers inflammatory markers & hospital costs.
2️- Fluid Resuscitation
  • Severe third spacing occurs due to fluid sequestration in the retroperitoneum.
  • IV Fluids (Lactated Ringer’s or Normal Saline) → Goal-directed resuscitation.
  • Monitor response via:
  • Urine output (goal: >0.5 mL/kg/hr).
  • Hematocrit (avoid hemoconcentration >44%).
  • Serum BUN (improving levels indicate adequate hydration).
Key Point: Early, aggressive IV fluids within 24 hours improves outcomes!
3️- Antibiotics
  • NOT recommended for routine use in acute pancreatitis.
  • Use only if infection is suspected (e.g., gas in pancreas on CT, positive cultures).
  • Infected necrosis treatment → Carbapenems (Imipenem/Meropenem), Metronidazole + Cefepime.
  • Percutaneous drainage & surgical debridement if needed.
4️- Calcium & Magnesium Replacement
  • Hypocalcemia is common due to saponification (calcium binding to fatty acids).
  • Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, QT prolongation).
  • Hypomagnesemia is common in alcoholics, requiring IV magnesium replacement.
5️- Oxygen & Respiratory Support
  • Hypoxemia is common (~30% of cases) due to:
  • Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
  • Pulmonary capillary leak → ARDS.
  • Monitor SpO2 closely.
  • Mechanical ventilation for severe cases with ARDS.
6️- Other Medications
No benefit for:
  • Octreotide, glucagon, anticholinergics, or aprotinin.
  • H2 blockers & PPIs → Only indicated for stress ulcer prophylaxis.
B. Endoscopic Management
  • Indicated for biliary pancreatitis due to gallstones blocking the ampulla of Vater.
  • Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) + Sphincterotomy →
  • Within 24-72 hours if evidence of cholangitis, sepsis, or persistent biliary obstruction.
  • Not needed if there is no obstruction (most gallstones pass spontaneously).
  • Cholecystectomy → Prevents recurrence in biliary pancreatitis.
  • Perform during hospitalization after pancreatitis resolves.
  • Interval cholecystectomy increases recurrence risk.
C. Surgical Treatment
Indications for Surgery

1- Infected Pancreatic Necrosis (Gas in pancreas on CT, positive cultures).

2- Persistent symptomatic fluid collections (Walled-off Necrosis, WON).

3- Large or symptomatic pancreatic pseudocysts (>6 cm, infection,

  • obstruction).

4- Severe sterile necrosis failing medical therapy.

Surgical Options
Minimally Invasive Drainage (Preferred over open surgery):
  • Percutaneous catheter drainage (CT-guided).
  • Endoscopic necrosectomy (for necrotic collections near stomach/duodenum).
Open Necrosectomy (For severe cases)
  • For extensive infected necrosis or failed percutaneous drainage.
  • Drains placed postoperatively for continued necrosis removal.
  • "Step-up Approach": Start with minimally invasive drainage before surgery.

Surgical Pseudocyst Drainage (Cystogastrostomy, Cystojejunostomy).

  • Indicated if pseudocyst persists >6 weeks & symptomatic.
Open Abdomen with Repeat Debridement
  • For severe pancreatic sepsis.
Prognosis & Outcomes
Overall Mortality: ~10%
  • Mild cases → <1️% mortality.
  • Severe necrotizing pancreatitis → ~50% if untreated, ~20% with surgical debridement.
Predictors of Poor Prognosis
  • Persistent organ failure >48 hours.
  • Necrotizing pancreatitis.
  • Respiratory failure, ARDS.
  • Hypocalcemia (due to fat necrosis & saponification).
Long-Term Complications
  • Recurrent pancreatitis (especially in biliary pancreatitis without cholecystectomy).
  • Chronic pancreatitis → Exocrine & endocrine insufficiency (diabetes, steatorrhea).
Pancreatic Ascites & Pancreatic Pleural Effusion

Pancreatic ascites occurs due to leakage of pancreatic fluid into the peritoneal cavity without signs of peritonitis or severe pain.

Causes:
  • Chronic alcoholic pancreatitis (most common in adults).
  • Traumatic pancreatitis (most common in children).
  • Chronic leakage from a pseudocyst or disrupted pancreatic duct.
Clinical Presentation:
  • Painless or mildly painful ascites.
  • Recent weight loss.
  • No response to diuretics (suggests a noncirrhotic cause of ascites).
Diagnosis:

- Ascitic Fluid Analysis (Diagnostic Paracentesis):

  • Straw-colored to blood-tinged fluid.
  • High protein (>2.9 g/dL, typically >4 g/dL).
  • Markedly elevated amylase (>1000 IU/L, often >5000 IU/L).
  • Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) → Identifies the site of duct disruption.
  • CT/MRI Abdomen → Evaluates the pancreatic duct, pseudocysts, or underlying chronic pancreatitis.
Treatment Approach:
Step 1: Medical Therapy
  • NPO (nothing by mouth) & IV Fluids.
  • Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) → To allow duct healing.
  • Somatostatin (Octreotide) → Reduces pancreatic secretions.
  • Serial Paracentesis (for symptomatic relief).
Step 2: Endoscopic Therapy (ERCP with Stenting)
  • Endoscopic pancreatic duct stenting to bridge duct disruption.
  • Partial duct disruptions → ~9️8% resolution with stent.
  • Complete duct disruptions → Only ~6️2️% success with stenting.
Step 3: Surgery (if medical & endoscopic therapy fail after 2-3 weeks)
  • Leak from pancreatic body/head → Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy.
  • Leak from pancreatic tail → Distal pancreatectomy ± pseudocyst drainage.
Pancreatic Pleural Effusion

A pancreatic fistula draining into the pleural cavity instead of the peritoneal cavity.

Clinical Features:
  • Chronic pleural effusion (usually left-sided).
  • Dyspnea, cough, chest pain.
  • Often misdiagnosed as recurrent pneumonia or tuberculosis.
Diagnosis:

Pleural Fluid Analysis (Thoracentesis):

  • Exudative pleural effusion.
  • Extremely high amylase (>3000 IU/L, often >5000 IU/L).
  • High protein content (>3 g/dL).
  • CT scan/MRI Abdomen → Identifies the pancreatic pathology.
  • ERCP → Confirms the pancreatic fistula site.
Treatment Approach:
Step 1: Medical Therapy
  • Chest tube drainage (for symptom relief).
  • NPO + IV Fluids + TPN.
  • Somatostatin (Octreotide) to reduce secretions.
Step 2: Endoscopic Therapy (ERCP with Stenting)
  • Bridging of the duct leak with a stent.
Step 3: Surgery (if conservative measures fail after 2-3 weeks)
  • Distal Pancreatectomy (if the leak is from the tail).
  • Roux-en-Y Pancreaticojejunostomy (for body/head leaks).
Chronic Pancreatitis

Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive, irreversible inflammation and fibrosis of the pancreas that leads to exocrine and endocrine dysfunction.

Key Features:
  • Chronic or recurrent epigastric pain (radiating to the back).
  • Pancreatic calcifications (seen in ~50% of cases).
  • Exocrine insufficiency → Malabsorption, steatorrhea, weight loss.
  • Endocrine insufficiency → Diabetes mellitus (~30%).
  • Most caused by chronic alcohol abuse.
Pathophysiology
  • Increased pancreatic duct pressure (~4️0 cm H₂O vs. normal ~1️5️ cm H₂O).
  • Ductal obstruction by stones and fibrosis → Progressive damage.
  • Destruction of acinar cells & loss of function.
  • Ductal dilation & calcifications ("chain of lakes" appearance on imaging).
Clinical Presentation
A. Symptoms
  • Chronic abdominal pain (deep epigastric, radiating to back, worsens with meals).
  • Pain relief by sitting forward or fasting.
  • Intermittent attacks of acute pancreatitis.
  • Steatorrhea (fatty stools, diarrhea, weight loss, vitamin deficiencies).
  • Diabetes mellitus (late-stage due to endocrine failure).
B. Signs
  • Epigastric tenderness.
  • Malnutrition & muscle wasting.
  • Jaundice (if bile duct obstruction occurs).
Diagnosis
1. Laboratory Tests
  • Serum amylase & lipase – Often normal or mildly elevated (due to pancreatic burnout).
  • Fecal elastase <200 mcg/g – Most sensitive test for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
  • 72-hour fecal fat test (>7% fat loss) – Diagnostic for steatorrhea.
  • Serum glucose abnormalities – Due to endocrine dysfunction.
  • Liver function tests (ALP, bilirubin) – Elevated if bile duct obstruction occurs.
2. Imaging Studies
  • Abdominal X-ray → Pancreatic calcifications (~5️0% of cases).
  • CT scan → Dilated ducts, fibrosis, and calcifications.
  • MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) → Evaluates ductal changes & strictures.
  • Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS) → Most sensitive for early disease, showing hyperechoic strands & calcifications.
  • ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography) → Identifies ductal strictures & "chain of lakes" pattern.
3. Chronic Pancreatitis Scoring Systems
  • Rosemont Criteria (EUS-based) – Classifies chronic pancreatitis based on parenchymal & ductal abnormalities.
  • Cambridge Classification (ERCP-based) – Grades mild, moderate, or severe ductal changes.
Complications
1. Pancreatic Pseudocysts
  • Fluid-filled sacs adjacent to the pancreas.
  • May cause pain, infection, or obstruction.
  • Drainage needed if >6 cm, symptomatic, or infected.
2. Biliary & Duodenal Obstruction
  • Fibrosis can compress the bile duct or duodenum.
  • Presents as jaundice, nausea, or vomiting.
  • Treatment: ERCP stenting or surgical bypass.
3. Diabetes Mellitus ("Pancreatogenic Diabetes")
  • Caused by loss of insulin-producing beta cells.
  • More prone to hypoglycemia due to lack of glucagon.
4. Pancreatic Cancer
  • Higher risk (~5x) in chronic pancreatitis.
  • Suspect in new-onset diabetes or weight loss.
Treatment
A. Medical Management (First-line)
  • Alcohol cessation (crucial for pain control & slowing progression).
  • Low-fat diet – Reduces pancreatic stimulation & steatorrhea.
  • Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) (e.g., Pancrelipase) – Improves malabsorption & pain.
  • Vitamin supplementation (A, D, E, K, B12) – Prevents nutritional deficiencies.
  • Pain management – NSAIDs, tricyclic antidepressants, pregabalin.
  • Diabetes management – Insulin therapy required (metformin is ineffective).
Role of Pancreatic Enzyme Therapy
  • Enteric-coated pancreatic enzymes (Creon, Zenpep, Pancrease, Viokace).
  • Reduces pain & steatorrhea.
  • Combined with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) to enhance absorption.
B. Endoscopic Therapy
Indications:
  • Ductal strictures → ERCP with stenting.
  • Pancreatic stones → Lithotripsy.
  • Biliary obstruction → ERCP with sphincterotomy.
C. Surgical Management (For Severe, Refractory Cases)
Indications:
  • Intractable pain despite medical therapy.
  • Biliary or duodenal obstruction.
  • Pseudocyst complications.
1. Drainage Procedures (For Dilated Ducts ≥7 mm)
  • Puestow Procedure (Lateral Pancreaticojejunostomy) → Duct opened and drained into jejunum.
  • Frey Procedure → Puestow + removal of inflamed pancreatic head.
2. Pancreatic Resection (For Small Duct Disease or Mass-like Head Fibrosis)
  • Whipple Procedure (Pancreaticoduodenectomy) → Used for head- dominant disease.
  • Beger Procedure (Duodenum-Preserving Pancreatic Head Resection).
  • Distal Pancreatectomy → For disease confined to the tail.
3. Total Pancreatectomy with Islet Autotransplantation (TPIAT)
  • For diffuse severe disease with debilitating pain.
  • Reduces pain but leads to brittle diabetes.
Prognosis
Exocrine Function:
  • Malabsorption persists in many cases despite enzyme replacement.
Diabetes Risk:
  • High risk after total pancreatectomy (~30-50% develop brittle diabetes).
Life Expectancy:
  • 10-year survival ~70%.
  • Lower in smokers & alcoholics.
Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
  • Pancreatic cancer is a highly aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis.
  • 3rd leading cause of cancer-related deaths (after lung & colorectal cancer).
  • Ductal adenocarcinoma (~80% of cases), mainly in the pancreatic head (~65-75%).
  • Rapid local invasion & early metastases (liver, peritoneum, lungs, lymph nodes).
  • Most cases diagnosed late → Only ~15-20% of cases are resectable at presentation.
Risk Factors
  • Smoking (2-3× increased risk).
  • Chronic pancreatitis (~5% risk over 20 years).
  • Diabetes mellitus (especially new-onset).
  • Obesity & high-fat diet.
  • Genetic predisposition (5-10%): BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome, Peutz-Jeghers, FAMMM.
  • Prior gastrectomy (>20 years ago).
